prs.title: Trace active Tokio worker threads with memory samples
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## What?

Record the number of non-idle Tokio scheduler worker threads alongside Turbopack's existing process-memory samples. The span-query API and MCP output expose it as the fourth value in each memory sample. The WebSocket query result adds a parallel worker series for visualization in [vercel/turbo-trace-viewer#33](https://github.com/vercel/turbo-trace-viewer/pull/33), retaining the original memory-only series.

## Why?

Memory samples alone do not show whether Tokio's workers were busy or parked at a given point in a trace. The aligned worker count makes it easier to correlate memory changes and traced work with scheduler activity.

## How?

Each traced runtime builder initializes one global atomic counter with its worker capacity, then Tokio's worker-only park/unpark callbacks adjust it. This avoids counting blocking-pool threads and assumes one traced Tokio runtime per process; shutdown bookkeeping is unnecessary for this metric. The counter is read at the existing memory-sampling cadence rather than emitting trace rows on each worker transition. Trace ingestion, span-query downsampling, and the WebSocket worker series preserve the count from the same sample as the selected memory value.

## Verification

- `cargo test --locked -p turbopack-trace-utils -p turbopack-trace-server`
- `cargo check --locked -p turbopack-cli -p turbopack-nft -p next-build-test -p next-napi-bindings`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`; `git diff --check`
- Not run: Next.js TypeScript/prettier/fu
…(truncated)

prs.title: [cd] Use pnpm to manage the version
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
lerna's last job was bumping the version, and it needed a dependency graph of exact pins to do it. Internal dependencies now use the `workspace:*` protocol instead, which pnpm substitutes for the concrete version when packing, so published manifests are unchanged.

`workspace:*` resolves to the same bare exact version that was pinned before.

That leaves the bump itself, which `scripts/version-bump.js` now does: write one version field per package, commit, tag. It stays small because every package is versioned in lockstep and releases always bumped all of them (`--force-publish`), so there is no changed-detection to reimplement.

`packages/next/package.json` replaces `lerna.json` as the version source of truth.
The release branch gate moves to `scripts/release-branches.json`.

Three things fall out:

- `normalize-version-bump.js` no longer has to normalize internal dependency specs, since `workspace:*` carries no version. Those specs also stop contributing to turbo input hashes.
- `set-preview-version.js` no longer needs to check out a branch first. That only existed because `lerna version` refused to run on a detached HEAD.
- no more lockfile regeneration after a release which means we can reuse n_m caches

`create-preview-tarballs.js` keeps `npm pack`: it rewrites internal dependencies
 to tarball URLs rather than versions, because that is what preview installs need, so pnpm's substitution would be the wrong transform. It now throws if any `workspace:` specifier survives th

prs.title: turbo-trace-server: speed up loading compressed traces
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Makes loading compressed (`.zst` / `.gz`) traces in `turbo-trace-server` much faster. On a large trace, compressed loads now beat raw loads from before this change. Raw loads get faster too.

| 12M-span synthetic trace (warm cache, median) | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| raw | ~17s | ~13.5s |
| `.zst` | ~26s | ~14s |
| `.gz` | ~26s | ~12s |

Smaller synthetic traces (2–3M spans) improve as well:
- raw goes from 3.5–4.9s to 2.2–3.3s;
- compressed goes from 2.2–3.7s to 2.1–2.9s.

### Why?

Opening compressed traces was very slow. There were two causes.

1. **Per-batch work was quadratic.**
   - After every batch of rows, `Store::invalidate_outdated_spans` cleared the cached corrected self time of **every** self-time event of each touched span, plus its ancestors and the root.
   - For a span with millions of events, that is a full scan per batch.
2. **Compressed input arrived in tiny batches.**
   - zstd/gzip decoders return about one input buffer of output per `read`, roughly 450 KB.
   - Raw files arrived in 64 MB reads.
   - So compressed traces ran that full scan about 100× more often. On the trace above, invalidation alone took ~12.7s for `.zst` versus ~1.5s for raw.

### How?

**Constant-time cache invalidation.**
- Each span now has a generation counter for the cached corrected self times of its self-time events.
- Invalidating a span just bumps the counter. A cached per-event value only counts if it was computed for the span's current generation.

prs.title: Turbopack: add turbo-trace-size CLI to inspect trace file size
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds `turbopack/crates/turbopack-trace-size`, a CLI (`turbo-trace-size`) that shows where the bytes in a Turbopack trace file (`.next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin`) go. It decodes the postcard `TraceRow` stream (raw, gzip or zstd) and reports:

- size per row type (`Start`, `Enter`, `Exit`, `AllocationCounters`, ...)
- the components of `Start`/`Event`/`Record` rows (name, target, values, fixed fields)
- bytes per span name, including its Enter/Exit/End/Record rows and Events
- bytes per attribute key
- the bytes spent re-writing the same span names, targets, keys and string values

```sh
cargo run --bin turbo-trace-size --release -- .next-profiles/trace-turbopack.bin --top 30
```

### Why?

`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING` traces get large quickly. This tool shows which events cause that, so we can decide what to slim down.

### Findings: `bench/heavy-npm-deps`, `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=1 next build`

68.42 MiB raw, 4.66 M rows (gzip -1: 21.3 MiB, zstd -3: 21.2 MiB):

| row type           |     count |     bytes |    avg |     % |
| ------------------ | --------: | --------: | -----: | ----: |
| AllocationCounters | 2,280,168 | 45.00 MiB | 20.7 B | 65.8% |

prs.title: Turbopack: fix turbo-trace-size test after MemorySample gained active_worker_threads
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Fixes the `rust check` (clippy) and `test cargo unit` jobs on canary, which fail with:

```
error[E0063]: missing field `active_worker_threads` in initializer of `TraceRow<'_>`
   --> turbopack/crates/turbopack-trace-size/src/lib.rs:936:13
```

The fix adds the missing field to the `TraceRow::MemorySample` row in the `turbo-trace-size` unit test.

### Why?

This was a semantic merge conflict between two PRs that each passed CI on their own:

- #99233 added `active_worker_threads` to `TraceRow::MemorySample`.
- #99765 added the `turbo-trace-size` crate, whose test builds a `MemorySample` row without that field.

Only test code is affected. Every other `MemorySample` constructor already sets the field.

### How?

The test row now sets `active_worker_threads: 3`. The size assertions are computed from the serialized rows, so they don't change.

Verified locally on top of `db03f83f`: before the change, `cargo test -p turbopack-trace-size` fails with the error above. After it, the following pass:

- `cargo test -p turbopack-trace-size`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` for `turbopack-trace-size`, `turbopack-trace-utils` and `turbopack-trace-server`
- tests of `turbopack-trace-utils` and `turbopack-trace-server`

prs.title: [ci] Increase deploy test concurrency to 8
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
Increases test concurrency for the deploy test jobs to 8 (prev: 2 in the full suite, 1 in new build-and-test jobs).

For deploy tests, the CPU-intensive work that should be as stable as possible (the Next.js build and server) does not happen on the runner. It happens remotely when the deployment is built at Vercel. The runner mostly handles I/O and setup: pushing the deployment, waiting for it to become ready, polling logs, and making requests against it. So the usual reason to cap concurrency (runner CPU contention) barely applies.

Adjusted rate-limits:
- 10x `api-projects-get` (prev failure: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/37617890690/job/112780953612#step:35:1159)

Trade-offs to watch:

- Peak concurrent Vercel deployments per run rises 4× (shards × 2 → shards × 8; 64 → 256 concurrent test files at today's shard counts). If we hit Vercel account deployment-concurrency limits, increase the limits
- maybe we still need a bit beefier runners if the concurrent setup/tests starve runner CPU

## test plan

- [x] [deploy tests with debug logging on this branch takes 30 minutes wall time without hitting Vercel rate limits](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/37627918534); usual flake on the 1st try (down from [97 minutes on canary](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/37588790388/attempts/1))

prs.title: create-next-app: write agent feedback block to AGENTS.md when enabled
prs.author: aurorascharff
prs.body:
### What

When `experimental.agentFeedback` is enabled, create-next-app now writes the `nextjs-agent-feedback` block into `AGENTS.md` along with the `nextjs-agent-rules` block.

### Why

Before this change, create-next-app enabled the flag in `next.config.ts` but only wrote the rules block. The feedback block was added later by `next dev`, and only when `@vercel/detect-agent` found a coding agent (`syncAgentFeedbackForDev` in `app-info-log.ts`). As a result:

- An agent that read `AGENTS.md` before running `next dev` never saw the feedback instructions.
- The block then appeared as an uncommitted `AGENTS.md` change on top of the "Initial commit from Create Next App".

### How

- `generateAgentFiles(root, { agentFeedback })` adds the feedback block after the rules block. The text is copied from `packages/next/src/server/lib/generate-agent-files.ts`, with a comment saying to keep them in sync. `next dev` compares the block byte-for-byte.
- `create-app.ts` passes `agentFeedback: !example && agentFeedback`, because examples don't get `experimental.agentFeedback` written to their config.
- `--no-agents-md` still writes no `AGENTS.md`.

### Verification

I ran the new helper next to `next dev`'s `writeAgentFiles` + `writeAgentFeedbackFiles`, with the flag on and off:
- The output is byte-identical in both cases.
- `hasCurrentAgentRules` / `hasCurrentAgentFeedback` return true on create-next-app's output.
- Running `next dev`'s writers again on that output returns `unchanged`.

prs.title: turbopack: don't report unactionable 'stopping failed' warnings
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## What

Builds with the Turbopack filesystem cache didn't give useful output when the cache couldn't be written during shutdown, for example because of a read-only directory or a full disk. The build succeeded, but it printed a bare `Shutting down failed: <message>` which was not useful

Before:
```
Persisting failed during shutdown: Unable to write SST file 00000020.sst

Caused by:
: Permission denied (os error 13)te/var/folders/p6/ytr7tcts5ndf72xw136ky30m0000gn/T/next-install-6cb7b5bc6e3b95a18ae07aa856827db93efc662fe73934ecebae8de778735e0c/.next/cache/turbopack/v16.5.0-canary.2-2c48f075ef/00000020.sst`
Shutting down failed: A previous write operation failed with an unrecoverable error; no further writes are possible
```

Now:

```
WARNING: Saving the filesystem cache failed:
    Unable to write SST file 00000020.sst: failed to create file `/Users/lukesandberg/projects/next_2/next.js/test/tmp/next-test-1791392696220-115/.next/cache/turbopack/unversioned/00000020.sst`: Permission denied (os error 13)
```

The "Shutting down failed" error is gone and the filesystem cache error is slightly improved.

Also:
- **Compaction is skipped once a write has already failed.**  That avoids a second, redundant failure.
- **Database shutdown can't fail anymore.** Compaction errors during shutdown are logged as warnings.

prs.title: turbo-tasks-fs: Don't print NotFound watcher errors
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Stop the Turbopack disk watcher from printing `watch error … NotFound` for paths that vanish while notify is scanning them, and send the remaining watcher errors to stderr instead of stdout.

### Why?

In polling mode, notify's `PollWatcher` walks the tree with walkdir. When a directory is deleted between being listed and being opened or stat'ed, notify reports an `Io` error with `NotFound`. Deleting a large tree (`rm -rf`, a package install) produces a burst of these. A filesystem fuzzer saw about 4000 in two minutes. Each one was printed with `println!`, so a library was spamming the user's stdout.

These errors don't signal a correctness problem. The watcher already invalidates the reported path recursively, and the next scan reports the removal anyway. The fuzzer runs had no missed invalidations.

### How?

- A small private classifier recognizes notify errors of kind `Io` wrapping `std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound`. It matches on the structured error kinds, not on message text.
- The watcher thread skips the print for those errors. Batch invalidation and batch-delay scheduling still run for every error, so invalidation behavior doesn't change.
- Other notify error kinds, including `PathNotFound`, are still reported, now on stderr.

### Verification

- `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-fs --lib watcher::tests`: 19 passed, covering native and polling watchers in both recursive and non-recursive modes
- `cargo clippy -p turbo-tasks-fs --tests -- -D warnings`

prs.title: Fix telemetry delivery on Node.js 24
prs.author: devjiwonchoi
prs.body:
### Why?

Telemetry fails on Node.js 24 with this error before any HTTP request is sent:

```text
TypeError: RequestInit: Expected signal ("AbortSignal {}") to be an instance of AbortSignal.
```

Native `fetch` checks that `RequestInit.signal` is an instance of Node's native `AbortSignal`. The Edge Runtime ponyfill creates its own `AbortSignal` class: the name is the same, but the constructor is different, so the signal fails the instance check.

The telemetry transport retries once and suppresses the final error, so the CLI can exit successfully without delivering events.

The controller was introduced when Next.js supported Node.js 14.6. Next.js now requires Node.js 20.9 or later, where native `AbortController` is available on all supported versions.

### How?

Use Node's native `AbortController` so its signal matches `fetch`, preserving the existing timeout.

Verified real SDK HTTP delivery on Node.js 20.9, 22.6, and 24.1, and the five-second cancellation deadline. The patched CLI received HTTP 204 for all three upgrade lifecycle events; Snowflake persistence is not yet verified. The full repository build and test suite were not run.
